vignette:
He is seventy-seven now, a tall African man with the careful posture of someone who has spent a lifetime standing in front of assemblies, calling classrooms to order, settling disputes before they grow. He is still the principal of a small school, though he talks about the work now as if it belongs to a different version of himself. When he describes what happened, he does not begin with fear. He begins with duty. It was late afternoon, and most of the students had gone home. He had stayed behind to finish paperwork and speak with a teacher about exam results. As he locked the office and stepped into the fading light, two men approached him near the school gate. At first he thought they wanted directions or money for transport. Then one of them grabbed his jacket, and the other struck him hard across the face.

He remembers the shock more clearly than the pain. He remembers the smell of dust, the scrape of his shoes as he lost balance, the strange thought that the children must not see him like this. The men shouted at him, demanding his bag, his phone, his watch. When he hesitated, one hit him again and kicked him after he fell. He curled his arms around his head and heard himself pleading, not for his life exactly, but for the beating to stop. By the time they ran, taking what they could, he was left on the ground outside the school he had spent years trying to make safe.

In the first days afterward, he tells himself he is fortunate. He is alive. Nothing is broken. His wife cleans the cuts on his face and shoulders and tells relatives that he is recovering. At school he tries to joke with staff, saying old men should not be out so late. But even then something in him has shifted. He starts arriving earlier and leaving before dusk. He asks younger staff to walk him to his car, then feels ashamed for asking. If a student runs up behind him in the corridor, his whole body jerks before he can hide it. He becomes watchful in a way that exhausts him.

At night the assault returns with humiliating force. He wakes soaked in sweat, convinced for a few seconds that someone is standing over the bed. Sometimes he dreams he is back at the gate, unable to call out, his voice gone while the men close in. Other nights there is no dream, only a pounding heart and the certainty that he is unsafe in his own home. He gets up to check the locks again and again. The smallest sounds—a dog barking, footsteps outside, a car slowing near the house—pull him to the window. His wife tells him gently that he has checked the back door already. He knows she is right, but knowing does not quiet him.

He notices changes in himself at school, where he has always taken pride in being calm and fair. He used to keep his office door open so students could come with their troubles. Now he prefers it shut. He finds himself studying strangers through the window and asking the groundskeeper whether the gate is secure. During assemblies, if there is a sudden shout or the crash of a chair, his chest tightens and his mind goes blank for a moment. He hates that the students might see it. A boy once approached too quickly from the side to hand him a report, and he recoiled so sharply that both of them froze. He apologized at once, but afterward he sat alone in his office, staring at his hands, feeling as if the assault had stolen some private authority he had carried all his adult life.

His wife says he is no longer easy in the evenings. He sits with the television on but does not follow the story. If visitors come unexpectedly, he becomes tense and withdrawn. He used to enjoy weddings, church gatherings, staff celebrations. Now he makes excuses, saying he is tired or has school business. Crowds unsettle him. Young men loitering near a shop can ruin the rest of his day. He avoids the road by the school gate where he was attacked, circling the block instead, though it adds time and makes little practical sense.

More painful than the fear is the injury to his sense of self. He speaks often of respect, of being an elder, a principal, a husband who should be steady. Since the assault, he feels diminished. He is quick-tempered with small problems and then deeply guilty. He cannot concentrate on reports the way he once did; the words blur, and his mind drifts back to the sound of those men’s voices. Some mornings he sits in the car outside school gripping the steering wheel, willing himself to step out and be the man everyone expects. He still goes in. He still signs forms, settles disputes, greets teachers. From the outside, much of his life remains intact. But he moves through it as if danger is waiting just beyond the edge of every ordinary day.
